tip: 'He has' in the north is ‘mae ganddo fo’, a form of ‘gan’ (with) that changes by person: ‘Mae ganddo fo gar newydd’ = he has a new car.
‘waeth’ is the irregular 'worse', from ‘drwg’, not ‘drygach’. ‘na’ means 'than': ‘waeth na heddiw’ = worse than today.
The ‘-a’ ending gives an informal command to one person: ‘caria’ means 'carry on' to someone you know well.
The ‘-id’ ending forms a past with no stated doer: ‘credid’ means 'it was believed'. ‘Credid bod y tŷ'n hen’.
‘bydda i'n’ is the future 'I will': ‘Bydda i'n anfon e-bost’ = I will send an email.
‘meddwl y byd o’ is a set phrase for 'think the world of': ‘feddwl y byd ohoni’ = think the world of her.
‘hen’ goes before its noun and softens it: ‘car’ becomes ‘gar’ in ‘hen gar’ (old car). Most adjectives instead follow the noun.
Add ‘-ach’ for 'more': ‘pwysig’ becomes ‘bwysicach’ (more important). ‘na’ means 'than': ‘bwysicach na gwybodaeth’.
‘dylwn i’ means 'I should', used for obligation: ‘y dylwn i orffwys’ = that I should rest.
An adjective after a feminine noun softens: ‘coch’ becomes ‘goch’ in ‘ffrog goch’ (red dress). Masculine nouns leave it alone.
‘wrth i’ sets up 'as' for a background action: ‘Wrth i'r haul fachlud, trodd yr awyr’ = as the sun set, the sky turned.
‘wedi’ before a verb makes 'had done': ‘wedi torri’ = had broken. So ‘Roedd y car wedi torri’.
‘pe bai’ sets up an unreal 'if': ‘Pe bai mwy o amser, byddwn i'n darllen’ = if there were more time, I would read.
‘yn hytrach na’ means 'rather than' before a choice: ‘Yn hytrach na mynd allan’ = rather than going out.
‘mwyaf’ means 'most' and comes before the adjective: ‘llyfr mwyaf diddorol’ = the most interesting book.
‘gwell’ is the irregular 'better', from ‘da’ (good), never ‘daach’. ‘llawer gwell’ means 'far better'.
‘na’ means 'than', but use ‘nag’ before a vowel: ‘yn gyflymach na'r bws’ (faster than the bus), ‘mwy nag ugain’ (more than twenty).
The linking ‘a’ means 'who' or 'that' and softens the verb: ‘triniodd’ becomes ‘driniodd’ in ‘a driniodd’ (who treated).
‘o’ (of) triggers soft mutation, so ‘defaid’ becomes ‘ddefaid’: ‘llawer o ddefaid’ = many sheep.
‘oddi wrth’ means 'from' a person or source: ‘oddi wrth y cyngor’ = from the council. Use it, not ‘o’, for senders.
‘cafodd’ is the irregular past 'got' or 'received', from ‘cael’: ‘Cafodd Gwenllian y swydd’ = Gwenllian got the job.
‘y’ (the) softens a feminine noun: ‘cath’ becomes ‘y gath’ (the cat). Masculine nouns stay unchanged after ‘y’.
‘pan’ (when) triggers soft mutation on the verb: ‘clywais’ becomes ‘glywais’ in ‘pan glywais i’ = when I heard.
The linking ‘yn’ softens the adjective after it: ‘cul’ becomes ‘gul’, giving ‘yn gul’ (narrow) and ‘yn beryglus’ (dangerous).
‘fy’ (my) triggers nasal mutation: ‘teulu’ becomes ‘nheulu’ in ‘fy nheulu’ (my family).
‘newydd’ before a soft-mutated verb means 'have just done': ‘Dw i newydd blannu’ = I have just planted.
‘mai’ (southern ‘taw’) flags the stressed word: ‘Er mai bach yw'r pentref’ = although the village is small, with ‘bach’ stressed.
The ‘-wyd’ ending forms a past with no named doer: ‘diddymwyd’ means 'were abolished'.
For emphasis, put the subject first with ‘sy'n’: ‘Yr Wyddfa sy'n denu’ = it's Snowdon that attracts.
‘ar’ changes shape by person: ‘arna i’ (on me), ‘arnat ti’ (on you), ‘arno fe’ (on him). Say ‘arnat ti’, never ‘ar ti’.
